speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the years, we have been making changes to the criminal justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have set out some of these changes in a handout.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can access this and other handouts I will be distributing later, through the MP@SGPARL app as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can see that since 2010, we have made several changes to improve our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are around 20 sets of proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They cover law enforcement, criminal investigations, court processes and sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In my speech, I will cover two major aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After my speech, two of my colleagues will be speaking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam will deal with the rest of the Bill, including changes related to Police powers to conduct searches and the criminal disclosure regime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling will also deal with some of the main changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essentially, if you are guilty, you should face the penalty for the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are innocent, you should go free.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first part, there has to be an effective framework of laws that deal with the crimes committed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that means there must be a strong and effective law enforcement system and there must be a Judiciary which can apply the laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second part, the criminal justice process must be fair and civilised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the approach that has been taken by my predecessors and I have continued along the same path.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The results are the safe and secure Singapore we have today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whenever we talk about criminal law, every country will say they are trying to find the right balance between the interests of society on the one hand and the individual's rights, on the other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think as we look around the world, there are serious questions as to whether the balance is being struck right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, we also try and strike that balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There can be differences on whether we are getting the balance right and we do need to be continuously mindful about that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is our approach and that gives context to the changes we are making.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will also speak briefly about a related part of the Bill, on the Sentence for Public Protection (SPP).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will apply to offenders who are 21 and above, at the time of the commission of the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will cover dangerous offenders who commit serious violent or sexual offences and provided there is an assessed risk that they may commit similar offences after they are released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The relevant offences will be set out in a new Schedule to the CPC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will include culpable homicide, attempted murder, rape and sexual penetration of minors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The SEPP is different from normal prison sentences under existing law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With normal prison sentences, offenders serve a fixed term of imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The usual process is that the offenders are released earlier, after serving two-thirds of their sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be no early release or remission.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court will also say whether the offender is released and at the end of the minimum term, will be subject to a review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if he is released, conditions can be imposed, until it is assessed that he is safe to be released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say a little bit more about how the SEPP works later on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, first, let me first explain why we are introducing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some people have asked is it because there has been an increase in serious violent and sexual crimes in Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The answer is no, that is not the reason for the SEPP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We looked at them and decided that it made sense to have something similar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, as in other places, serious sexual and violent crimes do occur, except that our numbers are much, much lower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are very serious offences and some victims, they are very young.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And some offenders can be assessed to have a risk of re-offending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2013, an offender was released from prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He had been put in jail for raping his six-year-old stepdaughter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was released after 12 years, which is taking into account the usual one-third remission period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After he was released, the offender moved in to live with his sister and her young granddaughters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2015, just two years after being released, he started sexually assaulting one of the young girls.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She was 10 years old at that time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The girl then moved out, but he did not stop.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2017, he sexually assaulted the girl's younger sister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2022, the Court sentenced the offender to the maximum 20 years of Preventive Detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court said that his risk of sexual re-offending was high.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But our society takes a very serious view of it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The impact on the young girls is devastating.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to deal with this kind of menace and protect our society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A few weeks ago, a man was sentenced to twenty-nine-and-a-half years in jail, for raping his niece.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For four years, he sexually assaulted her, almost every week, when she spent weekends at his home.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also gave her a sexually transmitted disease, and body-shamed her, until she developed an eating disorder.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is absolutely cruel what was done to the young girl.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The girl is now in a welfare home, undergoing counselling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She is facing psychological trauma as Members can appreciate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a handout containing more such examples, from Singapore and abroad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can see for themselves the kinds of troubling conduct and patterns of serious abuse, with persons offending repeatedly, sometimes, very shortly after they are released from prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our response to these kinds of cases is SEPP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the normal prison sentences, these offenders go free after serving their prison terms, even if there is an assessed risk that they might go out and do bad things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the day of release, if responsible people assess that the person might go out and commit a serious crime, nevertheless, the person has to be released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take the first example I gave Members, of the man who sexually abused his two grandnieces.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court said at the time of sentencing that his risk of sexual re-offending was high and sentenced him to the maximum 20 years of Preventive Detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what if there continues to be an assessed risk after he has served the 20 years?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the current law, he will have to be released: no conditions and no risk assessment is done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the SEPP, there can be a more calibrated approach to better protect society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be an assessment at the end of the minimum term to see if it is safe to release such offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This brings me to my next point: how will the SEPP work?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When one of the Scheduled offences is committed, the Court decides whether to impose a normal sentence or the SEPP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When deciding on the appropriate sentence, the Courts can look at risk assessments by IMH and, of course, such other reports as the Court decides are necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Defence can also make representations and submit expert evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Court assesses that the offender poses a risk to others, it can impose the SEPP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Court also retains the discretion not to impose the SEPP, for example, where it would be “gravely disproportionate” in all the circumstances of the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After this minimum period, the offender will be released if he is assessed to be suitable for release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This assessment will be made by the Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister will be advised by a Detention Review Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Board will be made up of relevant experts, for example, retired judges, lawyers, psychiatrists and psychologists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The offender and his lawyers can make representations to the Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, there is a Life Imprisonment Review Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Board advises the Minister on whether to release prisoners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are prisoners who have been sentenced to life imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, say, the offender is assessed to be suitable for release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He will be released on licence and conditions can be imposed on him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The conditions could include mandatory counselling, electronic monitoring or curfews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He will continue to be assessed until a view is taken that the conditions can be removed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the meantime, we will support his integration back into the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the other hand, if the assessment is that the offender should not be released, he will continue to remain in custody.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister must then review the offender’s suitability for release annually.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if he is eventually found suitable for release, he will be released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, we hope that this will enhance public protection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An offender who continues to pose a real danger to others should not be released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We really ought to deal better with cases like that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An offender sentenced to SEPP will have a very strong incentive to take his rehabilitation seriously in the first period of sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, he jeopardises his chances of being released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if he wants to be released after the minimum period, he will have to show both psychologically and through his behaviour that he is a changed person, that he can behave well and he does not need to be kept in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, tremendous incentive for a person to work on his rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These things can only work if the person who is the subject of the rehabilitation really puts in the effort.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, as I mentioned earlier, the SEPP allows for a more calibrated approach to sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take the examples I had mentioned earlier in the handout – egregious facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A sentencing judge might think, “This person is a monster.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Better not take the risk with a short sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Better to lock him away for a long time.” So, you do see some sentences, 20 years, 30 years, even more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the SEPP, the sentencing judges will now have more assurance, greater clarity, because the sentences they impose are only the minimum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be a further risk assessment with experts at the end of the minimum term.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CT and PD were introduced in 1954 to deal with recalcitrant offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since then, rehabilitation programmes have become widely available to all inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In particular, CT has become qualitatively similar to imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have decided to do away with CT and adopt characteristics of both CT and PD in the new SPP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SPP will be a useful sentencing option to deal with persistent or habitual offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: FMEs broadly consist of physical medical examinations, collection of body samples and taking photographs of body parts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These processes have now become very important for getting evidence in offences like rape and sexual assault.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will highlight two key aspects of the FME framework in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, we take a differentiated approach towards accused persons and victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, accused persons, one approach; victims, a different approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court can also draw adverse inferences from an accused person’s refusal to undergo FMEs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, FMEs may still be conducted, if delays will result in the loss of evidence and the victim is not able to give consent within a reasonable time due to a physical or mental condition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This could happen, for example, where a victim is sexually assaulted, falls into a coma and has no prior authorised decision-maker to give consent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In many cases, time can be critical, especially for DNA evidence, because DNA can degrade very quickly, if it is exposed to the environment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Allowing FMEs to be taken in these cases is in the interests of both the victim and the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can make the difference between catching the culprit and him going free and, worse, committing more such offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be safeguards in place for both accused persons and victims to ensure that FMEs are conducted safely and sensitively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, only qualified medical professionals can conduct physical medical examinations and invasive medical procedures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before taking a body sample, the person conducting the FME must be satisfied that it will not endanger the subject.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the person undergoing an FME involving intimate body parts is a lady, the forensic specialist or Police officer carrying out the FME must also be a lady.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have consulted quite extensively in preparing this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many stakeholders have shared their views, including the Judiciary, AGC, law enforcement agencies, criminal lawyers, members of the Law Society and members of the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The feedback and suggestions have helped us to refine our policies and we have taken many of the suggestions on board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I thank all those who have participated and given their feedback, and I hope that Members today will support the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The changes will do much to strengthen our criminal justice system and make Singapore a safer place.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In Malay. :   Please allow me to recap what Minister Shanmugam spoke about earlier and outline the key principles that underpins Singapore's criminal justice system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government's objective for our criminal justice system is to ensure the safety of our people so that they can live their lives without worrying about their own safety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Singapore is one of the safest countries in the world, with a low crime rate, a fair and effective legal system, and a trustworthy police force.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is important for the well-being of our society and our economy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have always been ranked highly in terms of law and order and safety in international studies and surveys.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We achieved this through laws that are tough on crime, effective enforcement of laws by the police and other law enforcement agencies, and fair and effective criminal procedures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We need to strike a balance between the desire to protect individual rights and safeguarding the interests of society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also need to continually review and update our laws.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are about 20 sets of amendments under this Bill, covering various aspects of the criminal justice process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will give a brief explanation on the FME framework.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: FMEs generally consists of physical medical examinations, collection of body samples, and taking photographs of body parts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through such a process, the police can gather forensic evidence for investigation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Forensic evidence is key in the investigation of major crimes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Therefore, there should be an effective legal framework for FMEs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The key features of the framework are as follows.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, we take a differentiated approach towards accused persons and victims.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For accused persons, the police will have powers to require them to undergo FMEs, even if they do not consent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is because if a person is guilty, the person will most likely refuse to be examined, if given a choice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Reasonable force can be used to conduct the FME, as long as it does not involve intimate body parts or invasive procedures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It will be an offence to refuse to undergo an FME without a reasonable excuse, and the accused can be imprisoned or fined, or both.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The court can also draw adverse inferences from the accused person's refusal to undergo FMEs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the case of victims, consent is generally required.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is important to ensure that victims, especially those who were sexually assaulted, are handled sensitively, to prevent them from being traumatised again.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If there is no consent, the police generally will not proceed with the FME.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, there are several exceptions, for example, if the victim has fallen into a coma after being sexually assaulted and DNA evidence will degrade if it is not collected as soon as possible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The scope of exceptions to consent is stringent and the Police will implement such exclusions judiciously.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Police will also wait, as far as possible, for the victim to recover before obtaining consent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Currently, an offender who receives a prison sentence, will be incarcerated for a fixed term as determined by the Court, and must be released unconditionally after that period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, there is a small group of high-risk offenders who still pose a danger to the public at the time of release, such as serial sexual offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The law currently does not allow us to stop such offenders from being released from jail or impose any conditions for their release, even if they are likely to re-offend.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Just now, Minister Shanmugam cited several tragic and egregious cases where the offender commits serious crimes shortly after being released from prison and also referred to a list of such cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2020, an offender was convicted of committing sexual abuse on his girlfriend's eight year old daughter and nine year old son; both of whom had low IQs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The offender had sexually assaulted them, forced them to watch videos displaying sexual behaviour, and to commit indecent acts while recording them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The children obeyed him because they were helpless and afraid of the offender.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The offender began committing this serious offence just two years after his release from prison.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: He was previously imprisoned for sexually abusing his own four-year-old daughter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, SEPP can only be imposed for very serious offences, which will be set out in the legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These offences include homicide or murder, attempted murder, rape and sexual penetration of a minor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, there are strict prerequisites that must be fulfilled before SEPP can be imposed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Third, SEPP only applies to adult offenders aged 21 years and above at the time of the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is in line with our general approach to sentencing young offenders, where the main focus is on rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since SEPP is a sentence, the Courts will decide whether SEPP should be imposed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is usually done after considering the risk assessment report by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) which is done independently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Defence can also submit its own expert report.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Court procedures will be applied at this stage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An appeal can also be filed if the Prosecution or Defence is not satisfied with the Court's decision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court will retain the discretion not to impose SEPP, for example, if a less severe sentence can still achieve the goal of public protection.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is a matter of public protection and safety which is best decided by the Minister, and not the judge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Minister’s power under SEPP is also in line with existing regimes such as Corrective Training (CT) and Preventive Detention (PD), and for life imprisonment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The power of the Minister is subject to safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In effect, the Minister's power is only to detain someone for one more year before the status is reviewed again.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Furthermore, the decision of the Minister is subject to judicial review.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There will be a Detention Review Board that will assess each offender under SEPP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Review Board will be made up of those with experience in forensic psychiatry or psychology, or experience with the criminal justice system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It may include retired judges and Judicial Commissioners, senior lawyers or psychologists and psychiatrists.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Offenders or their representatives, including family members or legal counsel, will be allowed to make a representation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: All relevant information will be provided to the Review Board, and in turn, to the Minister, including on the conduct and progress of the offender, and the risk assessment by a psychiatrist that will be done independently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A key safeguard, both at the sentencing and review levels, is an independent expert assessment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Such assessment will be done by psychiatrists using evidence-based scientific tools, which are internationally recognised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They will carefully evaluate various risk factors, including past violence; the level of understanding by the offender about his conduct and response to his treatment; and the support available to the offender upon release.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the Minister finds the offender suitable for release, the offender will be released on licence and subject to conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This could include mandatory counselling, electronic monitoring or curfews.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This period of release on licence balances the need to allow such offenders to return to live in the community, with the need to reduce threats to the public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will help offenders who are released on licence to return to society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, if an offender breaches the conditions of his licence or re-offends, he may be re-imprisoned and the Minister may revoke his release order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Once released with a licence, the offender will be reviewed at least once every two years, to monitor his progress.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If found suitable, the offender can be released unconditionally and the sentence ends.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Speaker sir, SEPP has many advantages, including enhancing protection for society against harm, promoting rehabilitation because offenders have strong incentives to improve themselves and fair punishment rules based on risk.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We introduced this regime after studying the issue carefully and concluding that it is necessary to better protect the public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have also discussed these amendments extensively, including conducting a public consultation in 2021, and have taken in the suggestions that were submitted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I will now speak about the amendments to law enforcement powers, the proposed provisions on criminal disclosure regime and other amendments to improve our Court processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These proposed amendments aim to strengthen our levers to tackle crime and enhance transparency, fairness and coherence in our criminal procedure laws.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Broadly, these amendments are intended to strengthen operational efficiency and investigative capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The first category of the amendments will update, enhance and clarify Police powers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Clause 10 empowers the Police to search suspects at the point of arrest, to detect and remove dangerous items from them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is to prevent arrested persons from possibly using these items to harm themselves or others, such as the arresting officers and passers-by.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Clause 3 removes the requirement for the Police to physically proceed to the crime scene when investigating arrestable offences, which, with advancements in technology and changes in the profile of crimes, is no longer always necessary or relevant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To be clear, the CPC currently already provides for circumstances where the Police need not investigate into arrestable offences and there is no change to this with the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Currently, the Police can already perform a search without warrant for arrestable offences in certain circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, if the Police have reason to believe that a suspect would be uncooperative or is likely to destroy the evidence before a search can be conducted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The difficulty is that it is not always straightforward for the Police to make such a determination at the onset.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Often, Police can only reasonably assess the cooperativeness of a suspect after having engaged him or her or sent the production order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Requiring that the Police do so in all cases is not practicable, as that would put the suspects on notice and allow them to tamper or destroy evidence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The amendment is a practical one that allows for more effective Police investigations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, they must be investigating an arrestable offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, the Police must have reason to believe that the document or thing is in the possession or control of a person, reasonably suspected of having committed the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This clause does not give the Police carte blanche powers to search anyone or anything.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It also does not give the Police powers to frisk or search individuals walking along the streets just because the Police find them suspicious.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The second category of the amendments will expand the powers of certain non-police law enforcement agencies (LEAs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Currently, only the Police and the officer from whose custody a person has escaped are empowered to pursue and arrest him.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, officers from CNB, the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) and Prisons can also play significant roles in arrest operations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For instance, ICA officers may come across the person at the checkpoint and can arrest him.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This amendment will enhance the joint Home Team operations and allow the Home Team departments to operate more effectively together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To give another example, clause 7 empowers non-Police LEAs to investigate bail and absconding offences arising from the predicate offences under their purview.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Currently, such officers have to seek the Police's assistance to investigate such offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For greater efficiency, the relevant LEA, which is more familiar with the details of the case, will have the powers to investigate the bail and absconding offences committed by the same accused person and arising from the case which they are investigating.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Moving on to the amendments on criminal disclosure, let me begin by providing an overview of our criminal disclosure laws.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2010, we introduced a framework for pre-trial disclosure in the CPC, namely the Criminal Case Disclosure Regime, which is commonly referred to as the "CCD regime".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The CCD regime formalised a framework for the Prosecution and Defence to sequentially disclose and exchange relevant information about their respective cases before trial.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This has led to greater transparency and consistency, and has been welcomed by all sides – the Judiciary, the Defence and the Prosecution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since 2011, a common law disclosure regime has developed in parallel through case law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Put simply, the Prosecution must disclose to the Defence unused material that may be helpful to the accused.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, under the Additional Disclosure Obligations (ADO), the Prosecution must disclose statements of material witnesses who are not called as Prosecution witnesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A "material witness" is one who can be expected to confirm or contradict the accused's defence in material respects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The ADO does not involve an assessment of the substance of the material witness's statement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It covers statements which may be adverse, neutral or helpful to the Defence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are overlaps between the KDO and the ADO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Where an unused material witness's statement is helpful to the Defence, it would have to be disclosed under the KDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2020, MinLaw commenced a comprehensive review of the criminal disclosure regime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It was necessary for us to study how the existing common law regime interfaced with the CCD regime, as well as the overall aims of disclosure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also considered how some areas of the common law regime, which had been left open by the Courts, should be addressed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Even though it was working well, we also considered improvements to the statutory disclosure framework, after having observed it in practice for several years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Disclosure is an important aspect of the criminal trial process and has significant implications on the pre-trial and trial process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It was especially important for us to study the practical aspects, including the possible implications on Prosecutors, Defence counsel, the Courts and law enforcement agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While the initial set of disclosure proposals were ready in early 2021, we took time to finalise them because of our extensive consultations with the various stakeholders, including the Defence Bar, the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) and the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These proposals were arrived at after extensive discussions with the Defence Bar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We presented the proposals to criminal practitioners and members of the Law Society in 2021, and they provided extensive feedback over multiple consultation sessions through to late 2023.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some of the proposals were adjusted significantly, following the feedback received.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While we did not agree with the Bar on every point, we explained the rationale for the proposals, and had candid and robust discussions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through this process, we were assured that the viewpoints and implications on the various stakeholders, including the Defence and the Prosecution, have been considered, to ensure that our proposed amendments are fair.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ultimately, the regime requires all stakeholders to play their part to ensure procedural fairness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Prosecutors are expected to discharge their disclosure obligations dutifully.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The AG has also said publicly that prosecutors take great care to comply with their disclosure obligations, in fairness to the Defence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will now take you through the proposed disclosure provisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The provisions will codify the common law position on: one, the scope of the KDO and ADO; two, the timing of the KDO; and three, the continuing nature of the KDO and ADO, among others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We recognise the importance of the KDO and ADO in ensuring fairness to accused persons, and this is why we are putting these obligations in legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have provided illustrations to help the public and parties understand what the obligations entail.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Moving the ADO to after the accused has committed to a defence, either in the CFD or in his testimony, is more consistent with the sequential and reciprocal nature of the CCD regime, where the accused will generally only receive material after filing the CFD.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I would also highlight that, statements of material witnesses that are helpful to the accused will be disclosed earlier, pursuant to the KDO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This would take place when the Case for the Prosecution (CFP) is filed, in CCD cases; or, in non-CCD cases, before the trial commences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Accused persons are expected to state their defence honestly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Generally, they would be able to do so, based on what they know.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, we also considered feedback, that there may be cases where accused persons decide to change their defence after obtaining new material disclosed under the ADO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There were concerns that, in cases where the new defence is a genuine one, which the accused could not have known about earlier, an adverse inference could be unfairly drawn against the accused.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We want to be clear, that accused persons will not be prevented from running a new or different defence, which was genuinely uncovered after the Defence obtained new material disclosed under the ADO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the accused decides to run a new or different defence based on new material disclosed under the ADO, he can explain his reasons for the change.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Court will consider the accused's explanation for changing his defence, and accordingly assess what, if any, inference should be drawn.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Accused statements come from the accused, and are, hence, different from other types of unused material which the accused may not know about.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The proposed rules are also consistent with the CCD regime, where accused statements which the Prosecution is not seeking to adduce as part of its case are required to be disclosed only after the accused has set out his defence in the CFD.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The second aspect of the disclosure provisions, in clauses 14, 15, 18, 19 and 22, involves fine-tuning aspects of the CCD regime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The CCD regime has been in place since 2010 and has worked well in promoting greater transparency and efficiency in criminal trials.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, we will remove the possibility of opting out of the CCD regime in State Courts cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, we will make it compulsory for the accused to file a CFD, after receiving the CFP, in High Court cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As the CCD regime was novel when it was introduced in 2011, we took an incremental approach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When parties file the CFP and the CFD, this facilitates clearer identification of the disputed issues, which in turn, makes the trial more focused and efficient.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Given the complexity of trials in the High Court and the severe consequences involved, it is essential that parties can prepare for trial and assess their cases more fully.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The proposed provisions will also further fine-tune other aspects of the CCD regime.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As Members can see, the CCD regime ensures that the Defence receives material from the Prosecution before the trial commences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the whole, the proposed disclosure provisions reflect our commitment to ensuring transparency and fairness in criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Now, moving on to the last set of amendments under the Bill, which are the amendments to improve efficiency in our court processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This amendment will allow more accused persons to be released before trial, in appropriate cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There will be safeguards to guard against the risk of absconding.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The proposed amendments, build on past reforms and demonstrate our commitment towards building a fair and effective criminal justice system that protects society from crime.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I will cover three main areas in my speech: first, the amendments relating to the FME; second, on the criminal disclosure obligations; and third, on the SEPP regime.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the FME, I welcome these amendments that will help preserve evidence crucial to solving serious sexual and violent crimes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was volunteering as the board member of a crisis shelter for survivors of domestic violence, some of whom are victims of violent crimes as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These amendments are important to assist the Police and our investigating bodies in administering FME.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially where there are grounds to believe that a delay in carrying out the FME may result in the loss, degradation, or contamination of the evidence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would this be done in consultation with advice from medical professionals, for instance, as to the probability of the victim waking up from coma or would the default position be to obtain consent from the victim's next of kin or authorised decision-maker?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would Police officers or persons conducting the FME go through any sensitivity or trauma training to handle the situation with tact, taking into consideration any cultural or religious sensitivities, especially when interacting with decision makers, parents or spouses of victims?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, on facilities to aid conduct of FMEs, in a Parliamentary Question in 2017, MHA stated that the Police issued sexual assault examination kits to hospitals with 24/7 obstetrics and gynaecology (O&G) specialist clinics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There was also a collaboration on the One Safe Centre for reporting within 72 hours of assault.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, can selected general practitioners (GPs) conduct FMEs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Family doctors who have treated and established a long-standing relationship with the victims' family may know the full history of the victim or the family members and thus the victim may be more comfortable with that particular doctor.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This FME by the doctor, of course, can be conducted in the presence of the Police or their own FME experts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fourthly, what are the efforts to encourage more victims to come forward to report so that they receive professional help and, at the same time, secure the evidence through FME?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The European Union (EU), in adopting the Istanbul Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, stated that according to research, it is good practise to carry out FMEs regardless of whether the matter will be reported to the Police and to offer the possibility of having samples taken and stored appropriately so that the decision as to whether or not to report the assault can be taken later by the victim.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Due to the stigma and criminal proceedings that will ensue, some victims may not come forward in time or come forward at all.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We perhaps need our clinics or centres equipped as a safe zone reporting shelter for victims to get medical, psychological and legal counselling, and FME with evidence to be secured and retained for investigation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fifthly, may ask if our offices of medical practitioners are provided immunity from personal liability in the conduct of FME on the victim?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, would medical advice on the exact FME procedure and any related risk be explained to the person so that he or she will be able to make an informed decision?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Dr Jack Lee, in his article in the Singapore Law Review, provided various recommendations on such safeguards by considering the degree of encroachment into the suspects bodily integrity, dignity and privacy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is classified into: one, non-intimate and non-intrusive procedures; two, intimate non-intrusive procedures; three, intimate intrusive procedures; four, prohibited procedures; and fifth, general safeguards.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do the Police or relevant related agencies have an internal guideline for such safeguards in FMEs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If so, would non-intimate procedures or non-intrusive procedures be prioritised or preferred in the first instance?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I now move on to criminal case disclosure.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a long time coming, following the Nabill Disclosure Obligations decided in 2020 and the Kadar Disclosure Obligations decided in 2011.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the Nabill case, the Court of Appeal deliberately left open the question of whether the prosecution would be required to disclose the prior statements of a material witness, where such witness is called to testify as a prosecution witness.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This issue finally came up for consideration in the case of Pigg, Derek Gordon vs the Public Prosecutor and the High Court held that a prosecution witness' prior statements can fall within the KDO obligations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even though such statements are presumptively inadmissible, this decision is also consistent with orbital expressed by the Court of Appeal in earlier decisions as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In what circumstances would the prosecution have an obligation to disclose such prior statements?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are offenders able to obtain legal representation during the review board hearing?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the views of the victims' families or public interest be considered before an offender is released from SEPP?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And lastly, whether the sentencing advisory panel has any role to play in determining the ambits and types of offences that may fall within the SEPP in the future?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will first talk about what I see as improvements and then touch on some provisions of concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The three improvements I will touch on are first, pre-trial release on personal bond; second, codification of prosecution’s duty to disclose unused materials; and third, compensation orders for victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 12 will amend section 93 of the Code, to make it more explicit that certain accused persons can be released on their own personal bonds and not need to find a bailor to post bail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will apply at both the stage when the law enforcement agency is managing the case, as well as later, when the accused is charged in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By making the option of being released on personal bond very explicit, it is likely that law enforcement agencies and the Court will release more accused persons on personal bond.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is especially meaningful for suspects who are poor and cannot find bailors of means to post bail for them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I had highlighted during the debate on the Workers’ Party (WP)'s Justice Motion in November 2020, not being able to post bail will usually result in job loss and devastating consequences on the family.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, such pre-trial detention would affect the person’s ability to prepare his defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had also highlighted that to address any concerns, conditions could be imposed when releasing a person on his own bond, such as reporting requirements, maintaining employment and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This amendment goes towards levelling the playing field between the rich and the poor in the criminal justice process and I commend it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, codification of prosecution’s duty to disclose unused materials.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 23 introduces a new Part 10A to the Code, entitled "Prosecution’s Obligation to Serve Certain Materials on the Defence".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The new provisions basically seek to import into the Code certain principles that have evolved through recent Court cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the debate in 2020 on the Justice Motion, the Leader of the Opposition had also suggested that codification of this obligation be done for greater clarity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By importing these principles into the CPC, it would be easier for law enforcement, Prosecution, Defence and also the general public to access them and to understand what is expected.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The third improvement I would like to highlight is in clause 40.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This concerns the Court’s powers in a criminal case to order compensation to the crime victim.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 40 amends section 359 of the Code to increase the chances of compensation being awarded in a criminal case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are positive moves to ease the pain of victimisation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 7 will introduce the new Part 4 Division 5 of the Code, which will govern FMEs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note the framework set out for the conduct of FMEs both on victims and suspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The provisions will facilitate obtaining evidence of high value to solve crimes, and include some safeguards to ensure that trained professionals conduct FMEs with regard to privacy concerns.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of non-invasive FMEs, the proposed section 40I provides that reasonable force can be used by authorised officers to extract the samples if the accused is uncooperative.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the proposed section 40I(2), such an authorised officer includes an auxiliary police officer (APO).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we are aware, APOs are trained mainly to conduct security activities and to assist police in maintaining law and order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Involving APOs in the use of force to extract body samples from accused persons is a highly confrontational investigative process which carries significant risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There has been some public concern about the introduction of the SEPP – and justifiably so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, an SEPP inmate could spend the rest of his life behind bars, based on a prediction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In assessing the SEPP, I note at the outset the following safeguards in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, whether to invoke the SEPP would be decided by the sentencing Court and not the Ministry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The judge will make this decision aided by risk reports submitted by the Prosecution and also by the Defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These offences generally include serious sexual crimes but also non-sexual violent crimes where death or grievous hurt is caused.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, even if the case falls within the Seventh Schedule, the judge need not invoke the SEPP and can instead decide to proceed with other sentences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The judge may assess that an SEPP sentence is not required to protect the public; or, as explained by sub-section 9 of section 304B, the judge may also decide that there are special reasons not to impose the SEPP, such as when a lesser sentence is adequate or when an SEPP sentence would be gravely disproportionate to the circumstances of the case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I reiterate that the SEPP is a severe sentence that should be invoked only in the most extreme of circumstances and there are compelling reasons for this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, even within the offences listed in the Seventh Schedule, such as those involving death or grievous hurt, these could arise in circumstances where the offender may not be dangerous in general.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such scenarios could include one-off incidents of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, or a case of a family member not taking steps to stop another person in the household from causing the death of a child or vulnerable person.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In such cases, the usual sentence for the offences should suffice, as these sentences are what Parliament has approved as appropriate for the crimes concerned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although risk assessment tools have become more sophisticated over time, and some argue are more reliable today, the risk of false positives will always be there.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We therefore run the risk of over-detaining someone based on a wrong prediction of dangerousness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I note the efforts by the Government to clearly scope the application of the SEPP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The SEPP provisions apply to a restricted class of offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, it seems from the Ministry’s pronouncements that the SEPP is targeted at a small handful of offenders who may have psychiatric disorders like paedophilia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even so, I call on the Courts and the Ministry to be circumspect when assessing the clinical assessment reports, as they are not infallible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, whether a person deemed dangerous at age 50 will be equally dangerous at age 70 deserves intense scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, in such cases of multiple charges, judges can already order the offender to spend the majority of their lives in jail, using long-established and accepted sentencing principles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would, to me, be preferable and would attract less controversy than leaving it to the executive to determine when an offender should be released.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand the rationale of protecting the public in the scenarios described.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In view of the limited class of offences involved, and the judicial safeguards I mentioned earlier, I feel constrained to offer my cautious support for it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have highlighted in my speech three positive aspects of the Bill, regarding the release of persons before trial on personal bond, prosecution's duty to disclose materials and on compensation for crime victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, I have concerns about the role of auxiliary police in FMEs and the SEPP regime.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Overall, the WP is in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The new framework for FMEs will certainly help our police force to solve crimes more effectively and accurately.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am hopeful it will also serve as a deterrent and reduce the incidences of crime.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, the SEPP is indeed suitable for dangerous offenders who are at risk of reoffending after release from prison.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Members of the public, in particular vulnerable potential victims of violent or sexual crimes must be protected from such criminals.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Numerous past cases have shown that despite time in prison, despite counselling or therapy, certain offenders, upon completing their sentences, continue to pose a threat to our community.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They remain unsuitable for life outside of prison.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it is the right decision to keep them detained.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, in some other countries, such as South Korea, Poland, even some states in the US and more recently Thailand, these offenders are given the option of chemical treatments to reduce the risk of re-offending.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Countries such as Germany and the Czech Republic also offer other long-term, permanent surgical options.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is internationally renowned as being a safe place to visit, live, work and to do business, and it is important that we continue to protect and uphold the systems and structures that instil this reputation and trust in Singaporeans and foreigners alike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My clarifications and suggestions are categorised into two areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: FMEs involve the collection of physical evidence to support investigations and legal proceedings, including in sexual abuse matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased to see that the Bill provides sensible guidance on the timely and sensitive collection of forensic evidence, while protecting the rights of both alleged victims and accused persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed legislative additions also satisfactorily cover issues such as consent, explanation of procedures and the roles and functions of police and medical practitioners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Children and vulnerable adults undergoing such an examination may well be distressed, scared and confused, and it is essential that we do all we can to protect the emotional and physical well-being of these people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: VCC volunteers work with the Police to support victims of crime, including victims of sexual crimes or other serious offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The volunteers, and I quote from their website, "are trained to provide a listening ear and to look out for these victims who may be struggling to cope in the aftermath of trauma".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The scheme is, however, currently only available to those who ask for assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps it may be appropriate for the scheme to be more widely promoted and actively offered to all victims of crime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, perhaps it may be appropriate to locate VCC volunteers within the OneSafe Centre, the one-stop abuse forensic examination centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In such situations, can the victim seek an FME without making a formal Police report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that some countries offer examinations independent of any obligation to report the matter to the police.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Forcing anyone to undergo a medical procedure to which they do not consent, raises issues of autonomy, dignity and the authority of the state and should not be undertaken without rigorous checks and balances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important that people who do consent to an FME have the legal capacity to do so and are provided with sufficient information to give informed consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, I also seek clarifications about the processes that are in place to (a) ensure that people are fully informed about what their FME will involve; (b) guide those who may have limited understanding of what they are consenting or not consenting to; and (c) protect those who may lack capacity to give informed consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, sensible to consider what measures are needed to protect the public from such dangerous offenders, and the proposed changes afford this protection in a number of ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Certainty in law is paramount to ensuring justice and, by providing a single sentencing model with a range of levers, we can better deliver targeted interventions based on assessed risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This certainty needs to be articulated clearly to those who are sentenced under this order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Second, this sentencing option may serve as a deterrent, potentially preventing individuals from offending or reoffending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Third, capping the age for such sentences at 21 is a positive move, as this allows young people assessed to be at low risk of reoffending the option of rehabilitation within the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In light of the evolving crime and criminality landscape it is necessary to protect the public from dangerous offenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In the process of doing so, it is equally important that we balance crime control with due process rights and rule of law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These principles stand as the cornerstone of our sentencing system and serve as a guide for determining consequences for those convicted of an offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On the principle of rehabilitation, I do seek clarification on where those on SEPP are to be housed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Prison Service has evolved into a leading correctional agency, embodying the principles of safe and secure custody, evidence-informed rehabilitation programmes, and effective community supervision for released prisoners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This group, known as mentally disordered sexual offenders, include sub-groups with significant psychiatric comorbidities, including psychotic disorders, personality disorders, intellectual disabilities and substance abuse disorders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, Circles of Support and Accountability, implemented in Canada, some regions of the United States, England, Wales and Scotland, are a community-based restorative initiative that aims to prevent further offending by offenders, including sexual offenders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill seeks to enhance Singapore's criminal justice system by introducing measures to strengthen crime-fighting capabilities and granting more authority to the Police and other LEAs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I am concerned about protecting the rights and interests of vulnerable individuals, particularly those with disabilities or special needs or those with limited education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These may be the accused or they may be victims of the crime.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of these vulnerable persons may not fully understand or be able to articulate their thoughts and feelings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Others may not grasp the implications of their actions due to their disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some are also at risk of being exploited or coerced into illegal activities, such as acting as drug mules or committing crimes under the influence of others.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even when they speak what they believe is the truth, some of them may not comprehend the consequences of their words or actions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, it is crucial to safeguard their safety, dignity, rights and well-being while maintaining the integrity of the legal process.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are well-recognised best practices for protecting the rights, dignity and well-being of vulnerable persons within criminal justice systems everywhere.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, investigations should employ specialised interview techniques that are trauma-informed, age-appropriate and sensitive to disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, interviews should be conducted in a safe and supportive environment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For several years now, the Singapore Government's Appropriate Adult Scheme has allowed independent, trained volunteers, that is, the Appropriate Adults (AAs), to accompany young or vulnerable individuals during interviews with LEAs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, there is also a best practice where personnel are trained in handling disabilities and other vulnerable persons, training for persons within the Police force, medical teams conducting, for example, the forensic medical examinations, and agencies like the Public Defence Office.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Vulnerable individuals must have access to legal representation who understands their specific needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is essential to provide specialised training for law enforcement and the judiciary on how to handle cases involving such individuals sensitively.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These training programmes should be mandatory, ongoing and available both in person and online.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Ideally, specialised units with experts in child psychology, geriatrics, disability services and trauma should be created to offer advice, assistance and referrals in investigations involving vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Last of all, the best practice of interagency collaborations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Interagency coordination and collaboration should be further enhanced to provide appropriate and streamlined support for vulnerable persons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, the participation rate and useability of the Ministry of Social and Family Development's Developmental Disability Registry could be improved to aid the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another possibility is this: for incarcerated individuals with developmental and other related disabilities, appropriate facilities should be established, separate from those for typical offenders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can tap on the learnings in Singapore from the youth rehabilitation programmes run by Trybe, remove the age limit and learn from them a good rehabilitation programme, and also halfway houses operated by various social service agencies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The move to codify the long-standing Kadar obligations derived from common law, for example, will give statutory footing to criminal disclosure practices that AGC and defence lawyers have already been practising for many years.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This having been said, I am concerned with three of the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The first is the new sentencing regime under SEPP.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The second is the expansion of Police powers as regards carrying out searches without warrants.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The third is the amendments related to FMEs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The CT and PD regimes apply to repeat offenders whom the Court believes may continue to be a threat to the public if they were to be sentenced per the sentencing frameworks for the offences currently before the Court.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
