text: The Court substitutes the sentences they would have received for their offences with a separate term of incarceration, that includes rehabilitative measures during the period of incarceration and that may include supervised early release into the community.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are two important features of these regimes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, the terms are imposed by the Court after having considered all of the evidence before it, including expert reports.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, there is finality to the terms, that is, they are a for a fixed duration so there is certainty as to the period of incarceration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The SEPP, on the other hand, is quite different.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, there is no certainty as to the period of incarceration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This jars with at least what is my understanding of the process of the larger process of how sentencing comes about.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Parliament enacts laws that define both offences and the punishment for them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These punishments are often enunciated as ranges of fines and/or imprisonment terms and are based on Parliament's view of the severity of each offence and what the offender needs to do to fulfil the retributive angle of justice.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The punishments are balanced against other offences across laws and updated from time to time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When an offence is committed, the Courts look at the range of punishment prescribed and the facts of the matter, determine the severity and apply a sentence within the range.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Where the sentence includes a term of imprisonment, there is a single point term, which presents the maximum time that a person may spend in prison.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The prisons may apply restitution, such that the offender actually serves less than the actual sentence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But there is a single-point sentence that the offender knows he will not go beyond.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The idea is that the Courts determine the punishment commensurate to the offence and once that person has completed his sentence, his retributive debt to the state can be considered to have been satisfied and he can reclaim his liberty.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: With the SEPP regime, however, an offender could continue to be deprived of his liberty even up to the duration of his natural life, even after he has paid his retributive debt and not by decision of the Courts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My second concern is precisely this, that the power to continue to deprive this person from his liberty lays in the hands of the Executive and not the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am curious and would like to seek clarification from the Minister as to why the regime was structured in this way, instead of following the regime for the safe custody of a person acquitted for unsoundness of mind under section 252 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Under the Penal Code, any person found to be of unsound mind at the time of the commission of an offence is to be acquitted.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such a person, having been found by the Court to be of unsound mind should naturally be assessed and be considered for remaining in the custody of the Government as he may pose a threat to himself or to people around him.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, section 252 provides that the Court is to order that such persons be kept in safe custody and reported to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Within one month, a designated medical practitioner is to assess that person and propose measures to be taken to minimise the risk of him causing harm to himself or to others.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister may then make one of several orders, including continuing to confine that person for a period not exceeding 12 months, provided that the total period of confinement does not exceed the notional sentence that would have been imposed on the person if he had not been acquitted for unsoundness of mind.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the event that the Minister assesses that the person should continue to be confined beyond the initial 12-month period, the Minister must make an application to the Court.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the decision to continue to confine the person remains with the Court.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If the SEPP was designed in a similar manner, it would have had to include just one additional step from the current regime proposed in the Bill, that the Minister would have to make an application to Court for each 12-month extension.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, this would be appropriate, as both regimes apply to extra-sentence situations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For section 252, there is, in fact, no sentence because the person would have been acquitted and for the SEPP, it would be further confinement after the minimum sentence had been completed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Must he be convinced beyond a reasonable doubt as a Court would have to be in imposing a sentence?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the hon Minister of State had said the approach by the Detention Review Board will be scientific and rigorous, and she had also shared some of the criteria.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But this is the report of the Detention Review Board.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: How would the Minister look at it and what is the standard that the Minister is expected to treat it?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, would the Minister also produce a publicly available report that will justify and explain why the offender should be further confined?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I also acknowledge that the SEPP would apply to a very narrow class of offences, those stipulated in Schedule 7.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These are very serious offences, like culpable homicide and rape.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I agree that the Minister's concern is very real.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, in comments that the Minister made to the media last week, he raised the same example he raised today of an offender who had served a sentence of 19 years jail and had been given 24 strokes of the cane for having committed statutory rape of his six-year-old stepdaughter and who, within three years of being released, had been convicted of then sexually assaulting two of his grandnieces and he was subsequently sentenced to the maximum 20 years of Preventive Detention.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If he was subject to an SEPP and had been assessed to not have been rehabilitated, he could have still be detained and we could have avoided having two additional innocent victims.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But the question that arises then is this: in whose hands should lay the power to deprive a person of his liberty?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My view is that it is the preserve of the courts and that the abdication of this prerogative should occur only in very narrow circumstances.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I can accept, for example, that in matters of natural security, where there may be urgency and because the Minister is himself the expert and also because of the grave consequences of delaying to act, that the Minister be empowered to take certain actions to detain certain persons.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But even in that situation, there are checks on the Minister's powers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Internal Security Act (ISA) provides a role of the President to play in detentions under that Act, including in some circumstances empowering the President to make decisions with personal discretion.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The bench is also involved in the advisory committee reviewing a detention under the ISA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But this important review and oversight function does not appear to be sufficiently articulated in the SEPP after the completion of the minimum sentence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is despite that the scenarios we would encounter in the case of an SEPP would not have the same urgency nor secrecy of information as we would see in the ISA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The reports for consideration as to whether to continue to detain an offender can be prepared in advance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There should not be concern over secrecy as this is a matter of public protection and the information regarding the offender would already be a matter of public record as he had gone through the court process at trial.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I had intended to seek the Minister's clarification on whether there would still be a role for the bench and lawyers to play, for example, in the constitution of the panel of experts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But Minister had pre-emptively already answered this when he said that retired Judges and lawyers would be included.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister consider that the chairperson of the panel should always be a member of the bench and that legal experts should also, as a matter of course be included in it?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Before I go on to the other two sets of amendments, I also do note that both the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary and the hon Minister of State had said that the Minister's decision is subject to judicial review and this provides some comfort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the illustrations in the Bill, the Police may search a suspect's place of residence without warrant.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, what are the safeguards that will be implemented to ensure that these wide powers are not abused?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, when would a person under investigation be considered to be a suspect on which the new provisions could be used and what would constitute "reason to believe"?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope these would be made public so as to allay concerns about how these powers would be wielded.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regard to FMEs, I am broadly supportive of the move to make it an offence out of the refusal to submit to an FME as part of Police investigations and for there to be adverse inferences drawn in the event that a person refuses to do so.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Again, I would like to ask the Minister what are the safeguards that would be implemented to ensure that such sanction of force is not abused.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In all three of these amendments, there could have been a greater role for the Court to play.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Fundamental to rule of law is the principle of separation of powers and the need for different parts of Government to check on each other.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, it is important that the Judiciary plays a role when there are wide powers granted to the executive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three sets of clarifications on the changes to the criminal case disclosure process and on the SPP and SEPP.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first set of clarifications is on the changes to the criminal case disclosure process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, upon the Defence's request, the prosecution must arrange for the defence to view the exhibit at a Police station or a prescribed place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The photograph may be just one of many pages in a long documentary exhibit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In such a situation, can the Minister clarify if it is open to the prosecution to serve a redacted form of the exhibit containing the image where the image is omitted?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Defence then only has to arrange to view the unredacted image in the exhibit at the Police station or prescribed place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may be a more proportionate approach where the Defence has a set of the rest of the documentary exhibit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify what is considered a “material” witness?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second set of clarifications is on how an offender’s suitability for SPP and SEPP will be assessed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the SPP, can the Minister share what other factors, apart from physical and mental conditions, will be taken into consideration when assessing an offender’s suitability for the SPP?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the factors for assessing an offender’s suitability for the SPP and SEPP are identical?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify whether there is any limit to the number of periods for which the court can remand an offender in custody under sections 304A(3) and 304B(5)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third set of clarifications is on provisions for offenders subject to SPP and SEPP.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what resources or programmes will be provided to rehabilitate offenders on SPP or SEPP?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What steps will be taken to mitigate the risk that being put on SPP or SEPP may signal that the offender is beyond rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if any frameworks will be introduced for the assessment by experts, review by Minister, and representations by the offender, at the end of the SEPP minimum period?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed amendments represent a significant move towards ensuring that our criminal justice system remains effective, fair and transparent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In recent years, several egregious cases that have highlighted the need for a comprehensive review of our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At its core, the Bill aims to strengthen the state’s levers to tackle crime, especially those that I mentioned earlier, and I will be speaking on three key aspects: first, introduction of new sentences for public protection; second, the FME Legislative Framework; and third, enhancing the powers of police and law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, on the new sentencing framework for public protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The impetus for the proposed law is apparent in wake of the alarming egregious cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As mentioned by the Minister earlier, in 2001, a diagnosed paedophile served a term of 19 years jail and received 24 strokes of the cane for the rape of his stepdaughter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Within three years of his release from prison, he sexually assaulted his two grandnieces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For his depravity, he was sentenced to the maximum 20 years’ preventive detention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And just last year, a man was sentenced to 18 years’ preventive detention and 12 strokes of the cane for, amongst other charges, aggravated sexual assault.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was also shortly after he had served his 16-year jail term for rape.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the new sentencing regime, it allows for the Courts to better protect the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also provides the necessary flexibility to strike a balance between punitive measures and rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry consider mandating such reports for all SEPP-related sentences?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that this would strike a better balance between the rights of individuals and the pursuit of justice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Further, the SEPP regime provides that if the offender is assessed to pose a risk to society and therefore would continue to be imprisoned at the end of the SEPP term, regular reviews will be done to assess their suitability for release.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry consider enshrining the frequency of this review into the legislation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would ensure that whilst the protection of the public rightly remains at the forefront, the individual rights and liberties of these offenders are still given due consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: FMEs are critical to bringing perpetrators to justice, especially in the case of sexual offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The time sensitivity of FMEs is paramount since forensic evidence can rapidly deteriorate, degrade, or become contaminated, leaving no viable substitutes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The FME, intimately connected with privacy, dignity, and the pursuit of truth, demands a careful recalibration of our legal approach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under the FME framework, the police now have the express power to require accused persons to undergo FME where relevant to an investigation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also an offence for accused persons to refuse to undergo the FME without reasonable excuse, and the Courts may also draw negative inferences in such cases if a trial is to be held.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry clarify under what circumstances would the refusal be done under a “reasonable excuse”?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are safeguards to the conducting of the FME, which include the requirement to ensure that there is no danger to the individual and the requirement for qualified medical professionals to conduct physical medical examinations and the collection of invasive samples, save for blood samples by way of pricking a finger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A key safeguard proposed by the Ministry is implementing measures to minimise leakage and unauthorised sharing of materials obtained through the FME procedure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry clarify what measures, cybersecurity or otherwise, it will take to ensure that these photographs are held in the utmost confidence?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the measures to protect against unauthorised collection of visual evidence such as photographs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Further, under the proposed section 40H, informed consent will generally be required from the alleged victims and/or their authorised decision-maker, depending on the age of the alleged victim.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry consider developing standardized guidelines for obtaining informed consent for FME procedures?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Further, under section 40H(1)(b), in the case where the alleged victim is between 14 and 16 years old, both the alleged victim and the alleged victim’s parent or guardian consent would be required for the FME.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry kindly clarify the rationale for this?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the context of criminal investigations, where time is often of the essence, it becomes imperative to equip the police and law enforcement agencies with powers that allow for swift and decisive action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are sculpting a legal framework that allows us, as members of this House, to protect the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Speaker Sir, notwithstanding the suggestions mentioned, I rise to support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.09 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) plays a crucial role in Singapore’s criminal justice system.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It outlines the processes and rules that govern the investigation, prosecution and adjudication of criminal cases within our legal system.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: A robust CPC ensures the protection of individual rights and safeguards and access to a fair and just trial.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It also provides legal certainty and predictability, outlines accountability of law enforcement and judicial authorities and contributes to social order and stability.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: When effectively and efficiently administered, it also plays a role in deterrence of criminal behaviour, respect for the rule of law and civil liberties, and strengthens public confidence in the administration of justice.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I have two sets of clarifications as part of the changes proposed in this Bill.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The first set of clarifications relates to the introduction of the new Division 5 – Forensic Medical Evaluation, of Part 4 of the Bill, under Information to Police and Powers of Investigation.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The second set of clarifications relates to the introduction of the new sections 304A and 304B, under Sentence for Public Protection and Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If this is not the case, could the Ministry clarify why the same consent standards may not apply to both alleged victims and accused persons?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the forensic setting, it remains the case that this is a medical evaluation, and I would like to seek clarification whether this will be considered the legal standard henceforth relating to consent of medical evaluations in general.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If this is not the case, I would like to seek clarifications from the Ministry why a forensic medical evaluation for alleged victims would be different from non-forensic medical evaluations in terms of allowable age of consent and the ages to which permission from a parent or guardian is required.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill appears to be more permissive to allow individuals to consent at a younger age by themselves from 16 years old rather than at 18 or 21 years old, at least to the alleged victim, based on the current proposed amendments.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: However, in this context, other than a retrieval of blood through a blood draw, which is considered as invasive, would it be possible to list the body samples that are considered non-invasive in the context of a non-consenting FME for greater clarity?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, would retrieval of other body samples like urine, saliva, head hair and root of head hair, sample of fingernail or toenail be considered invasive or non-invasive?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is not yet clear in the current amendment.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, to retrieve urine and stools, one would require access to intimate parts and, therefore, this is not allowed under section 40I but may I clarify what about hair, nails and saliva?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Would a probing swab to the mouth or nose for saliva or bodily fluids, or pulling of a hair sample at its root be considered invasive?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I begin by unequivocally and categorically stating that the crimes for which the proposed sections 304A and 304B cover are heinous, disgraceful and reprehensible in the strongest terms.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These crimes have a long-lasting impact on the victims, in terms of physical and emotional trauma, the psychological effects on their mental well-being, their loss of security and trust towards significant others, and how they potentially view current and future relationships as well.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In my work as a clinician, I also see victims of such trauma permanently scarred to the extent that they are unable to form meaningful relationships nor are they able to work, and some even struggle with the need for psychiatric support and longer-term therapy.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These crimes are abominable beyond measure and have no place in our society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: However, in deliberating this change and the introduction of these two sections, I take a leaf from the document “Sentencing in Singapore” guide published by MinLaw and MHA on their website, wherein it articulates four evergreen sentencing principles: deterrence, rehabilitation, proportionate punishment and prevention.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The same guideline also articulates the different types of sentences, including imprisonment, fines, caning, community-based sentences, corrective training, preventive detention and the death penalty, and that rehabilitative potential is also assessed in the context of Propensity for Reform as well as the Nature and Gravity of the Offence.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In these proposed sections, I would like to request clarifications over three areas, some of which have also been addressed by the Minister previously.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In our world of widespread Internet and electronic use, the potential of sexual crimes relating to use of intimate images, recordings and voyeurism, as well as gaining access to, producing, distributing and selling child abuse material do have potential for harm to the victims and members of the public not unlike some of the offences already highlighted in the Seventh Schedule.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, these offences, indeed, far outstrip the extent of impact and harm that current offences included in the Seventh Schedule may pose and I seek greater clarity on how these offences have been chosen.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Are current sentencing frameworks not enough to address adequately both retributive and restorative aspects of justice for the offenders today, no matter how egregious their crimes may be?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If the numbers are small, could we not consider a greater amount of resources, monitoring and enforceability for our community sentencing options, release orders, detention orders as well as employment placement and preparation schemes, rather than relying on the hon Minister’s discretion to detain such individuals up to the natural life of the prisoner, as in SEPP?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Could we structure interventions better and amalgamate the hybrid use of prison sentences with Community Orders, Mandatory Treatment Orders, use of electronic monitoring and Day Reporting Orders better?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These could still achieve the intended outcome of public protection and mitigate risk when employed with greater oversight and supervision.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If the numbers are, indeed, sizeable, then would it not be telling of how much more we need to do in conducting treatment, as well as rehabilitative and reintegrative programmes back to the community, especially for this sub-group of offenders of violent crimes and sexual harms?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I wonder whether there are alternatives possible and yet to be considered within the existing structure of our legal provisions to suitably manage the risk and still protect the public.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are fortunate to live in a society where the trust between administrators and citizens allows us to engage in critical discourse.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is our duty to question, deliberate and ensure that any changes to our legal framework are just, balanced, equitable and respectful of individual rights, even as we seek to protect the common good.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wish to make two main points on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would benefit this House for us to have a greater appreciation of the underlying problems that then called for this solution.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appreciate and understand the need for our Police Force to have levers that aim to protect the safety and security of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, searches without warrants have had unintended, negative consequences in some other jurisdictions with different operationalisation of this policy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The significant impact these measures have had on vulnerable communities in some such countries is worth noting.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some studies of warrantless searches and similar programmes have also found that persons of minority descent tend to be stopped more frequently than majority ethnicity individuals, even after controlling for variability and certain profiling estimates of crime participation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be important for us, as a society, to protect against profiling.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this continues to be true, given the extended powers and the impact it could have on the trust between our people and the Police force, if misused, even by accident, we must enquire about the safeguards in place to prevent potential unlawful use of this power and consideration on providing recourse to those who may feel unfairly searched.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the case of Mah vs AG, the appellant highlighted, in obiter dicta, that when a Police officer makes a decision, in this case, to make an arrest, his decision relies on his own common understanding, his own biases and his own experience as a Police officer.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even with the best of intentions, law enforcement is, ultimately, in the hands of individuals and, sometimes, things can go wrong, especially when officers are required to make difficult split-second decisions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What measures will be in place to prevent unfair accusations against Police officers as well who are discharging their duties?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that we have a sensible force and one that annexed their duties to the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I also ask that we consider the realities of the systems we design and the way they may impact vulnerable communities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If I understand it correctly, the proposed amendment to section 34 suggests that this search, on the other hand, is afforded to all officers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This individual discretion may open Police officers to accusations of biasness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A better protection could be for that permission to search perhaps coming from a higher rank.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The public would also be keen to know how these searches could be applied.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A search without warrant is performed in countries for some instances, such as the United Kingdom (UK), the United States (US) and India.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is usually performed with the caveat that it is done to save life and limb and prevent serious damage to property, including searches for weapons on a person.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, our Police have limited powers of search.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is unclear what the newer approach would be with this new power.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, members of the public who are vulnerable or face communication challenges, may have difficulty understanding this.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should they not be appropriately informed, processes to manage them should be in place to mitigate potential trauma or misunderstanding.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, the ordinary citizen has nothing to fear.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What we do want to prevent are anxieties introduced by the perceived loss of privacy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some further questions I have include, firstly, could MHA share with the House why the search without warrant amendments are being put forth now, the trade-offs considered and why this is needed when our Police force have long demonstrated their ability to be effective without this provision?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What protections will be afforded to citizens who believe they are being searched unfairly?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will an officer determine reason to believe and what are the standards?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be an opportunity for clarification before someone is deemed obstructive?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Who holds the authority to conduct searches or authorise searches for persons with special needs, for example, and how will special care be taken for these individuals?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My second point of concern pertains to the enhanced FME examinations, particularly in cases involving serious sexual offences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Victims are compelled to recall traumatic memories and it is not uncommon for them to take a considerable amount of time before finding the strength to speak up.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also little comfort to victim survivors if the perpetrator is released in just a few months.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All this is amidst the social stigma which many survivor victims face, despite such sexual assaults or violence not being due to their own actions but rather malicious perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Evidence provided by FMEs can be extremely valuable in constructing a case or, conversely, could be exculpatory, should a suspect be found not guilty of the crime.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In either scenario, I agree that the FME constitutes an integral part of the Police procedures and toolkit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Newspapers have reported on some of these cases.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Time is of the essence for law enforcement services.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Medical evidence, such as DNA, is time-sensitive and can degrade, potentially being washed away by the accused, if given the opportunity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is crucial for law enforcement to conduct FMEs as expeditiously as possible to bring wrongdoers to justice.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In February 2000, Ms Chua, 27, was raped and found in Bukit Batok Nature Park with her clothes next to her.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She eventually succumbed to her injuries and her assailant was never apprehended.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such examinations can also solve cold cases, perhaps bringing some form of closure to family of victims who suffered years ago.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Questions arise about situations where an accused person may have a legitimate reason for refusal.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the legislation protect against possible unjust penalties for refusal?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will we advise victims or accused persons who are minors regarding the process in a way that is age-appropriate?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the considerations and processes for working with a victim?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, I would like to inquire about the procedures and practices in place for vulnerable individuals, particularly those with special needs, to ensure that their circumstances are appropriately addressed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's safety is a collective achievement, built upon the support and understanding of our citizens, the hard work of men and women who are in law enforcement.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Safety is often cited as a key reason why many of us are grateful to live in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are well aware that this sometimes requires the relinquishment of certain rights.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, we must ensure that the vulnerable are protected and that law-abiding citizens can go about their lives with confidence, secure in the knowledge that they are well-protected.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we navigate these amendments, let us uphold the principles that have made Singapore safe, such as justice and fairness and respect for each other's rights.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We owe it to our citizens – everyday Singaporeans who are law enforcement officers as well, and to future generations, to ensure that the laws that we enact strike a delicate balance between security and liberty.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But I have some clarifications that I hope the Minister will be able to address.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, my concerns are about the new rules for the conduct of FMEs and SEPPs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I will speak, first, on the new proposed rules on FMEs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: FMEs are conducted to obtain forensic evidence which is critical for investigations, particularly those pertaining to serious sexual offences, such as rape.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As MinLaw has explained in its press release of 10 January, FMEs are generally seen as an important aspect of modern evidence-gathering and there are simply no substitutes for certain types of specific forensic evidence, for example, when penile swabs need to be taken from accused persons in sexual assault cases, in order to show proof of contact.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These types of evidence are also time-sensitive because they may be lost, degraded or contaminated over a short period of time.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: All these factors speak in favour of a robust FME regime, but there is also a need to balance these concerns with respect for personal autonomy and notions of consent.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My first clarification for the Minister relates to the information that is provided to alleged victims in the course of procuring their consent.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In order for any kind of consent to be valid and legitimate, an individual must be given sufficient, accurate and relevant information on the actions that are to be taken and on the implications of these actions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister provide details on the kinds of information that Police officers will be required to provide to alleged victims when seeking out their consent to carry out FMEs?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On this point, is the Minister able to share the guidelines that are in place for Police officers to determine whether delays in the conduct of FMEs will result in the loss, degradation or contamination of the evidence concerned?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister explain how the Police will be trained to determine if delays in carrying out the FMEs will, in fact, result in the loss, degradation or contamination of the evidence?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The explanatory statement to this Bill also refers to a very wide range of conditions that include dementia and learning disabilities, both of which are conditions that can be experienced very differently in terms of severity.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, a medical diagnosis of dementia does not immediately equate to a loss of capacity.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And under our Mental Capacity Act, a person must be assumed to be able to make decisions for themselves, unless it is established that they are unable to do so.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On this broad point, I seek three clarifications.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, what training will Police officers be given to enable them to decide whether a person suffering from a particular physical or mental condition is actually unable to give their consent?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The new FME rules under the proposed section 40H of CPC also list the conditions under which the Police must seek consent from the alleged victim's parent, guardian, deputy or donee, if the alleged victim is personally unable to provide their own consent.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The consent of such representatives is, however, not required if delays in carrying out the FME will result in the loss, contamination or degradation of the evidence and the consent cannot be obtained despite all reasonable efforts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister clarify, what the threshold is for such reasonable efforts and how this term would be interpreted?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, would the term be confined to physical attempts to locate the alleged victim's representative; or would it also potentially apply to a situation where the Police are unable to convince the alleged victim's representative to grant their consent?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If the legislation is meant to include the latter situations as well, what are the qualitative factors that are then taken into account by the Police when they decide whether or not reasonable efforts have been made?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The threshold of reasonableness, once again, comes into play for FMEs conducted on accused persons, further to the proposed new section 40I of the CPC.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, reasonable force may be applied by authorised officers where intimate parts and invasive procedures are not involved.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I seek clarification from the Minister on the kind of standard that will be applied in determining what exactly constitutes such reasonable force.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this point, is the Minister able to explain how a subject's gender identity will be accounted for and respected?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: What will the treatment be for subjects who identify as non-binary in gender?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister could provide some clarification on how these kinds of matters would be approached.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I will now move on to the proposed SEPP.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is introduced under the new section 304B of CPC.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that the threshold for imposing an SEPP is a very high one.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Amongst other things, the SEPP regime only applies to offenders aged 21 and above at the time of the offence, and the Courts must be satisfied that it is in the interests of the protection of the public that an SEPP be imposed.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the minimum term, the offender will not be automatically released.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But, instead, will only be freed if assessed to no longer pose a threat to the public.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This assessment will be made by the Minister for Home Affairs, based on the advice of an expert panel.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are extremely severe provisions and I seek three clarifications from the Minister on them.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, will any clear sentencing guidelines be issued to encourage consistent sentencing by the Courts under the SEPP regime?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, what kinds of rehabilitation programmes will an offender be required to attend?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In 2022, the UK House of Commons Justice Committee issued a Report on Sentences of Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPPs).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a scheme in the UK that is somewhat similar to SEPP.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In the Report, a joint submission was made from 50 psychologists, psychiatrists and psychotherapists who had experience of working with people serving the IPP sentence.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In that submission, various forms of psychological harm were identified as having emerged from the imposition of an indeterminate sentence.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The submission states, and I quote, "More recent studies find that people serving an IPP sentence consistently describe mental and emotional deterioration caused by the sentence, including feelings of depression and hopelessness, feeling very anxious, symptoms of paranoia and psychosis, suicidal urges and feeling fundamentally "changed" for the worse".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A study by the UK Ministry of Justice in 2021 noted that, "The rate of self-harm in people serving an IPP sentence is around double that of people serving a life sentence and almost double that of people serving a determinate sentence." In light of the higher potential for mental health issues among SEPP prisoners serving indeterminate sentences, rehabilitation programmes should be available in quantity and they should be accessible to offenders in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I seek the Minister's clarification on the kinds of rehabilitative treatment and mental health support that will be made available to SEPP prisoners as well as their family members.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My third clarification has to do with how the new SEPP regime gels with victim-centric approaches to criminal justice, especially in the realm of violence against women.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In 2014, the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) issued a report to MinLaw entitled AWARE's Recommendations on Sexual Assault Law in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In that report, AWARE put forward the view, based on its own research and work, that the most urgent priority for policies tackling sexual violence is to improve the processes for investigating cases and achieving convictions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In the experience of AWARE’s Sexual Assault Care Centre as reported in the 2021 AWARE paper, An Omnibus on Gender Equality, formal reports are not made in 70% of cases of sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am given to understand that victim-survivors may choose not to report their cases due to fear of harm or revenge from perpetrators or because they are concerned about the impact of the reporting on such perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These may be people who are known to them or even be family members.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These concerns are actually quite unrelated to the severity of the actual punishments that are meted out to offenders.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In more extreme cases, if punishments are overly harsh, victim-survivors who are the subject of coercive control might hesitate to come forward in the first place to report that offences have been committed against them.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The robust criminal justice system that we have today is due to our LEAs which work tirelessly to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I note that this Bill contains comprehensive proposals spanning enforcement, sentencing and Court processes which reflect the Government's continuous efforts to ensure our criminal justice processes remain fair and effective in an increasingly complex security landscape.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I support this Bill, but would like to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is sensible, as it synergises inter-departmental capabilities to better deal with flight risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I have noted the past success and risk of joint operations involving not just HTDs but also other LEAs outside MHA, such as Singapore Customs under the Ministry of Finance (MOF).

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, can the Minister clarify if such powers will or can be extended to LEAs beyond the Home Team to further strengthen inter-Ministry operational efficiencies?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Clauses 4 and 6 clarify the powers of LEAs in obtaining customer information from financial institutions (FIs), in line with Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)' policy, specifically for banks and licensed companies, to enhance the protection of confidential customer information held by these FIs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the safeguards for the protection of such information procured from such FIs during investigations, including the deletion of such information after investigations have concluded?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I now turn to the new framework for FMEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, for victims where FME is needed, consent is required except in certain circumstances laid out in the proposed section 40H(2) of clause 7.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, can the Minister clarify, for cases where an FME is conducted on a victim above the age of 14, who is unable to give consent due to a temporary physical or mental condition, for example, intoxication, but who upon recovery refuses consent, does he/she have any recourse for the removal of FME information or perhaps, upon conclusion of investigation and Court proceedings?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For both frameworks, the judgments by the Court will be complemented with timely assessments of an offender's rehabilitation closer to the potential release date and powers vested upon the Minister to, on the advice of a Review Board, order the offender's release on licence or continued detention.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As it is critical for such powers to be exercised judiciously, based on robust risk assessments, so that decisions fairly balance the continued detention of an offender with the need for public safety, can the Minister clarify the safeguards that will be put in place?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, what criteria would the Minister or Review Board consider in assessing an offender's suitability for release?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two, what are the grounds for the offender's application for the judicial review against the decision of the Detention Review Board?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Aligned with this objective to enhance public protection and to provide greater assurance, I note that the amendments do not apply to those who are already serving existing sentences.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What can be done to better protect the public in cases where an offender who was sentenced before SEPP came into effect but still poses a threat to the public and will be released upon serving his current sentence?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is just like the example the Minister mentioned about the offender who was sentenced for raping his niece and, after less than two years upon release, sexually assaulted his stepdaughter.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While I appreciate that an aim of this measure is to expedite cases to relieve stress on our criminal justice system, the contrary may result if the risk of abscondment is not properly managed.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: With this in mind, can the Minister share the rate of abscondment for cases of personal bond in the past five years and whether key learnings were or can be derived from dealing of these cases to strengthen safeguards against flight risks?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I recognise that clause 33 accords immunity to the Chief Justice and the Selection Committee regarding the appointment of members to the Panel of Psychiatrists, introduced in the Criminal Justice Reform Bill that was passed in 2018.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to bear in mind that such cases of sexual abuse or assault on young persons can have a long-term adverse impact on the victims and we must do all we can to protect them and prevent these crimes from even taking place again.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When it comes to serious violent offences, such as culpable homicide and attempted murder, the danger posed to society is even clearer and greater.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a country, we would have failed these victims who fall prey to offenders who were released at the end of their jail terms even though they showed signs of reoffending.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Home Affairs Minister, in his response two years ago, had shared that MHA and MinLaw were, in fact, studying a new sentencing option to give more protection to the public.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think we can all agree that in such egregious cases, there needs to be a balance struck somewhere, to allow offenders to have a second chance while also keeping the vulnerable protected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to echo feedback that I have received from lawyers who regularly handled such cases, that we would need more clarity on how the assessment will be conducted and what are the criteria for an unconditional discharge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also hope that to be fair to offenders, there can be additional and dedicated resources provided to support offenders convicted under SEPP in their rehabilitation journey while in prison.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I think we can all agree that in such egregious cases, there needs to be a balance struck somewhere, to allow offenders to have a second chance while also keeping the vulnerable protected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to echo feedback that I have received from lawyers who regularly handled such cases, that we would need more clarity on how the assessment will be conducted and what are the criteria for an unconditional discharge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also hope that to be fair to offenders, there can be additional and dedicated resources provided to support offenders convicted under SEPP in their rehabilitation journey in prison. : I believe that the amendments are much needed and timely, and I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the Bill seeks to bring about a series of changes, my speech today will focus on clause 304B, which provides for SEPP.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the outset, I acknowledge the Government’s calibrated approach for the SEPP, the applicability of which is scrupulously limited to serious violent and sexual offences specified in the Seventh Schedule.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my view, one of the most severe legal punishments – indefinite detention in prison – is being rightly and proportionately reserved for the most deplorable species of offences.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That said, the nuance that bears highlighting is this – it is not necessarily just the intrinsic nature and severity of the Scheduled offences themselves that warrant the infliction of the SEPP, but perhaps more crucially, it is the proclivity of the offenders to re-offend after they have been released.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have read in news reports and judgments of cases, the atrocities committed by some offenders.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We surely must have asked ourselves – could this have been prevented, or prevented from happening again?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each victim is one too many; each victim has physical and mental trauma that he or she may never recover from in spite of their best efforts and support from their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Minister Shanmugam has said: "the Government’s key duty is to protect the public." It is certainly also a key duty of this House to do the same.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding, we must discharge this duty responsibly and proportionately.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After all, there is no saint without a past, and no sinner without a future.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The objective of the SEPP is not to eliminate the future or decimate the prospect of rehabilitation of any offender.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead, it seeks to ensure that offenders are not released back into society before they have been sufficiently rehabilitated, which could otherwise jeopardise the future of a potential victim.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To this end, I seek the following clarifications from the Minister: Firstly, during the period of continued incarceration, will SEPP inmates undergo specific or specialised rehabilitation programmes?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if so, whether good performers of such rehabilitation programmes can be allowed an avenue to make representation to seek for Minister’s early consideration for review of his suitability for an early release?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, in respect of sexual offenders who have been released unconditionally or on licence from SEPP, will MHA consider, apart from curfew and/or electronic monitoring, also imposing a condition akin to an automatic Protection Order that prohibits such offenders from coming into any unnecessary contact with their former victims?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And where the offender was diagnosed with pedophilic disorder, that he or she should also be prohibited from coming into any unnecessary contact with children?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the substantive amendments include the introduction of the SEPP for which many of the Members here have spoken much about.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the past few years, there have been many reports of cases involving dangerous offenders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These include serial sex offenders who preyed on children, as well recalcitrant offenders who committed serious sexual or violent offences soon after being released from prison.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is not just a statistic, it is a stark reality that poses an immediate threat to the safety and well-being of our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I should also highlight that it has the challenge of balancing the individual rights of those affected by the wide ranging enhancements placed to protect the public against such dangerous offenders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the introduction of the SEPP could see the offender jailed indefinitely, beyond the crime he was originally charged for, it is through these lens that I want to seek clarifications so that while we agree that we must better protect the public from such offenders, we also have the civic duty to be fair to such offenders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Clause 45 includes the "Seventh Schedule" for offences of which sentences for SEPP may be imposed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The offences cited include offences under sections 304, 307, 308, 326, 354, 375, 376, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes violent crimes such as culpable homicide, attempt to murder, voluntarily causing grevious hurt and serious sexual offences.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the SEPP be applicable to those already in incarceration?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In other words, if there is currently a violent or sexual predator already serving sentence, could the SEPP be applicable to him after it is deemed by MHA that the offender is still a threat to society?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If yes, do we have the necessary court resources to assess those that are already in incarceration?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If no, how do we prevent the current offenders who have a tendency to recommit crimes be detained for the sake of public safety?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While serving SEPP, does an offender still have opportunities to be rehabilitated and taken off SEPP before the end of his mandatory jail term?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Why does there seem to be an increase in number of such crimes in the first place?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are we committing any resources from any Ministry in order to better understand this at the causal level?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should we not be looking into preventing such heinous crimes from happening in the first place?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And is there adequate mental health support and rehabilitation services for such offenders who may have underlying mental issues?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For the sentencing for SEPP, I understand that it is up to the Courts to decide.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Minister has earlier shared the make-up of the panel in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Who will decide who sits on the panel?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And during the individual's detention, will the offender be able to appeal against the SEPP sentenced on him?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or will he only be re-assessed at the end of his mandatory detention?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the period where the offender is released on licence and placed on certain conditions, do we monitor such offenders in terms of their Internet use, keeping in mind online platforms are often gateways to groom and exploit potential victims?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For those already sentenced on SEPP and not released on licence, the Bill mentions regular reviews to determine whether the offender can be unconditionally released and the sentence brought to an end.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Who will be conducting these reviews and how often can such reviews be appealed?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill goes a long way in terms of providing legal measures that can help us work towards creating safer communities and protecting the most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to also ensure that we use a combination of prevention and rehabilitation programmes to tackle this at the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I support the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will first respond to questions regarding the law enforcement related amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked whether the powers to pursue and re-arrest persons who escape from the lawful custody of Home Team Departments will be extended to non-Home Team law enforcement agencies (LEAs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our assessment is that the extension of these powers to Home Team LEAs would suffice to effectively deal with persons who escape from lawful custody of Home Team Departments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At the same time, non-Home Team agencies may seek the assistance of the Police for persons who escape from their custody.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Ms Rahayu Mahzam, has answered the points raised by Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications from Members for Minister, Minister of State or Senior Parliamentary Secretary?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Looks like it was a very comprehensive response from the three office holders.      .
